proposer.mechanism: CHOP-REGIME COOLDOWN, layered on position-tier-gate (cap=1) verbatim. The exec algorithm tracks the timestamps of OPEN orders that the cap=1 gate has BLOCKED (using only its own deterministic accounting — no external data subscription). A blocked OPEN occurs when the oracle's CLOSE+OPEN pair fires at the same ts_init and the cache still shows the prior position — this is the dominant cap=1 activation path documented in the base PTG NOTES. We maintain a rolling deque of recent block timestamps and prune entries older than CHOP_WINDOW_NS (default 10 seconds). On each new OPEN that survives the cap=1 gate, we count the number of blocks in the last CHOP_WINDOW_NS: if that count >= CHOP_THRESHOLD (default 5 blocks in 10 seconds, i.e. >=50% of the last 10 oracle ticks were flip signals against an in-flight position), SKIP this OPEN as well — we are in a chop regime. Otherwise SUBMIT. CLOSE orders (is_reduce_only=True) always submit unchanged. The cooldown is not a fixed-duration timer; it self-clears as old blocks roll off the rolling window.
proposer.inefficiency_exploited: The base PTG NOTES explicitly identifies the loss-driving regime as 'high-noise days (20260312, 20260313, 20260316, 20260317) where the oracle flip-flops rapidly' — these are exactly the days where the cap=1 mechanism delivers its biggest absolute improvements over the simple baseline ($492.50, $264.00, $124.50, $166.50). On those days, the cap=1 mechanism FILTERS the same-ts_init OPEN but still allows the algorithm to take fresh OPENs at the next oracle tick when the previous position has cleared. If the oracle is still flip-flopping at t+1s, the new OPEN is itself part of the chop and is disproportionately likely to lose. The cap-block-rate IS the chop-regime indicator, computed entirely from the algorithm's own state without needing any market-data callback. When the algorithm has been blocking 5+ OPENs in the last 10 seconds, the oracle is signaling rapid reversals — the next OPEN that DOES survive the cap (because the prior position finally closed and 1s elapsed) is exactly the kind of trade that gets caught in the chop. By skipping those, we are likely dropping the worst-EV subset of cap=1-passing OPENs.
proposer.why_survives_costs: Mean slippage = 0 and commissions = 0 in this simulator (verified from base position-tier-gate backtest-results.json: mean_slippage=0.0, max_abs_slippage=0.0, total_commissions=0.0). The mechanism only adds a SKIP condition on OPEN orders that survive the cap=1 gate — no order construction, no order modification, no new order types, no passive orders, no subscriptions, no market-data dependencies. CLOSE orders submit unchanged so intraday_flat compliance is preserved. Runtime overhead: O(1) amortized per OPEN (one deque append + one left-prune). No risk of the delivery-channel failure that destroyed r4 (-3.1%) and rendered r5 inert (0.0%) — the signal source is the algorithm's own deterministic accounting, which cannot be throttled by the simulator's tick-delivery semantics.
proposer.builds_on: position-tier-gate (cap=1 retained verbatim as the first gate; chop-regime cooldown is an additive SKIP gate applied AFTER cap=1 passes, only for OPEN orders). Structurally distinct from all 5 prior PC runs: r1 (consensus filter on order directions, inert at K=5/0.6); r2 (loss-cooldown after realized_pnl<0, -6.1% because losses are i.i.d.); r3 (winners-run extend-close, -82% because oracle reversal signals are real); r4 (adverse-mom via quote_tick, -3.1% because quote_tick under-fires); r5 (adverse-mom via book_deltas, 0.0% because delta channel was also under-fire). This proposal's signal source — the algorithm's own internal cap-block accounting — has ZERO dependency on simulator-delivered sub-second market data, sidestepping the structural failure mode that broke 4 of the 5 prior attempts. Conditions on a regime signal (cap-block density) that the base NOTES explicitly identifies as a loss-cluster correlate.
proposer.alternatives_considered: (1) r2's loss-cooldown (trigger on realized_pnl<0 after a CLOSE): failed because losses are i.i.d.; doesn't capture regime. The chop-regime cooldown conditions on a different signal (cap-block density) that is empirically tied to a documented loss-driving regime. (2) r3's winners-run extend-close: failed because oracle reversal signals are real, not just noise. This proposal does not extend or skip CLOSEs — it only filters OPENs. (3) r4/r5 adverse-mom filters using quote_ticks or book_deltas: failed because the delivery channels under-fire in this simulator. This proposal avoids ALL market-data subscriptions entirely. (4) Time-of-day filter (skip OPENs in negative-aggregate time buckets): tested in r5's alternatives_considered, no robust buckets across dates. Overfit risk. (5) Randomized reduction (r5 criticizer suggestion): empirically tested in r5-round-2, pnl drops proportionally with trade count, Sharpe not improved. Declined. (6) Total-OPEN-rate cooldown (skip OPEN if more than N OPENs in last T seconds, where N counts ALL OPENs not just blocked): this is essentially trade-count throttling on the algorithm's own activity and would fire continuously since the oracle issues OPENs every second; doesn't capture regime. (7) Position-cap=2 or cap=3: structurally inert per base NOTES (oracle never holds >1 contract). (8) Chop signal from CONSECUTIVE blocks (a streak count) rather than rolling-window count: streak-based is brittle (one non-block resets); rolling-window is more robust. (9) Asymmetric chop (track block direction): adds parameters with no clear directional rationale — chop is direction-agnostic by definition. Declined.

objections.text: Empirical calibration disproves the mechanism's selectivity. I measured the cap-block-per-10s-window distribution on three train dates by reconstructing block events as (simple_positions_per_sec - ptg_positions_per_sec). Result: cap-blocks fire at approximately 1 per second nearly continuously throughout each session, even on low-volume days. On 20260316 (high-volume chop day): Pr(blocks_10s>=5) = 100% (every 10s window contains exactly 5 blocks). On 20260319: 100%. Even on 20260308 (lowest-volume day, only 253 ptg positions): Pr(blocks_10s>=5) = 98.2%. With the Proposer's default threshold of 5-blocks-in-10s, the SKIP rule activates on essentially every OPEN that survives the cap=1 gate — degenerating to 'skip ALL OPENs', which empirically reduces realized_pnl to roughly $0 (matching r3's catastrophic -82% failure mode where most OPENs were skipped). The mechanism's parameters do not select for chop regimes — they select for 'any session activity', which is uniform across the train window. This is the same calibration trap r2 and r3 fell into.

The cap-block event structure is not actually a 'chop regime' indicator — it is a 'oracle signal cadence' indicator. The oracle fires at 1Hz (signal_interval_seconds=1.0 in config). Each oracle tick that issues a CLOSE+OPEN pair with the cache showing the prior position is one cap-block. Since the oracle issues a signal every second AND the typical position holds at least 1 second (per r3 analysis: even short-hold positions average 1-2s), the cap=1 mechanism blocks ROUGHLY ONE OPEN PER SECOND throughout the entire session — completely independent of market chop. The cap-block density is determined by the oracle's fixed signal cadence and the deterministic netting mechanic, NOT by market microstructure. The Proposer's premise (cap-block density correlates with chop) is mechanically false — the empirical data confirms this with near-constant ~1/sec block rate across both chop and quiet days.

Near-duplicate of prior failed mechanism: this proposal is structurally equivalent to a uniform OPEN-skip rate filter. Since the chop-block-density signal is approximately constant across the session (per the empirical analysis above), the rule reduces to: 'after warmup, skip every OPEN that survives the cap=1 gate'. This is mathematically identical to r3's mechanism in its skip-everything failure mode. The Proposer's r3 analysis correctly identifies that randomized OPEN reduction (criticizer's r5 alternative) gives proportional pnl drop — confirmed empirically there. This proposal will likely produce a similar near-zero realized_pnl outcome.

Lack of empirical pre-validation. Of the prior 5 PC runs, the most disciplined was r4, which at least computed the expected uplift offline before implementing (+13.74% predicted, -3.14% live — divergence explained by the delivery-channel issue). r3 also did pre-validation (the duration-PnL correlation analysis) but failed because of a selection-bias confound. r5 inherited r4's offline number. This proposal has ZERO empirical pre-validation of the chop-cooldown signal — neither (a) the activation rate per the proposed threshold (which would have revealed the BLOCKING issue above before reaching debate), nor (b) the conditional PnL of cap-passing OPENs as a function of recent block density. After 5 failures, the experimental discipline bar is empirical pre-validation, not first-principles plausibility.

Superior alternative not considered: a different mechanism CLASS entirely. Five PC runs have demonstrated that OPEN-side filtering (whether by direction, by recent PnL, by hold duration, or by microstructure) does not beat the +5% gate on top of position-tier-gate. The robust empirical finding is that position-tier-gate IS at a local optimum on the strategy/cost-structure pair. A genuinely untried alternative class is execution-style modification — specifically, since slippage=0 and commissions=0 in this simulator, there is no execution-cost lever to pull. BUT: the algo could perform SHADOW execution analysis. Specifically, propose: a NULL/IDENTITY exec algorithm that runs as a layered observer to position-tier-gate, persisting per-order diagnostics to disk (via a write to results dir on on_stop) so that FUTURE iterations have the raw data needed for genuine pre-validation. This would not pass the gate (delta=0), but it would unblock future iterations on this experiment line. However, the spec says runs are scored on pnl/slippage and the proposal is restricted to algorithms that attempt to beat the gate — so this 'observer-only' mechanism is also unsuitable as a passing candidate. The honest conclusion is that this experiment line is exhausted, and the run-6 attempt should pivot to a fundamentally different framing — for example, exploiting the fact that intraday_flat is enforced by strategy (per r3 NOTES) to perform LATE-SESSION FORCED EARLY EXIT (skip OPENs in the last N minutes of session).

The Proposer's claim 'A blocked OPEN occurs when the oracle's CLOSE+OPEN pair fires at the same ts_init' is essentially correct but glosses over how the algo OBSERVES blocks. The algo's own on_order() handler returns without calling submit_order when the cap blocks — that's the block event, observable directly via the cap-check returning True. Implementation-wise this is fine, but should be specified as 'increment block counter inside on_order() at the point where net_qty >= position_cap, BEFORE returning' rather than reconstructed externally.

suggested_alternatives: LATE-SESSION FORCED EARLY EXIT: skip OPENs in the last N minutes of the regular session. Uses only deterministic wall-clock information (no market-data dependency). Hypothesis: end-of-session positions have less time to develop the oracle's 30s direction signal AND are more likely to be force-closed by intraday_flat at unfavorable prices. Empirically falsifiable: easy to pre-validate by reading positions.csv and computing PnL by hour-of-day bucket on the train window.

BLOCK-FOLLOWS-CHURN cooldown (different parameterization of the same proposal): trigger only when the block count in the LAST 1-2 seconds is anomalously high (>= 2 blocks in 2s), NOT averaged over 10s. This would condition on a tight burst pattern, which the 1Hz oracle CANNOT generate from the netting mechanic alone — bursts would only happen if the oracle issues sub-second flip signals during high-noise periods. But this requires actual measurement to verify the burst-vs-baseline density.

ABANDON layered filtering entirely. Run a final no-op variant (pure cap=1 with on_stop diagnostics persisted to disk) to give future researchers the raw observational data they would need for genuine empirical pre-validation. This is not a passing run but is the most informative single iteration if the experiment is exhausted on this axis.
criticizer.reasoning: Two BLOCKING flaws: the cap-block density signal is approximately constant across the session (driven by oracle 1Hz cadence + deterministic netting, NOT by chop), and the default threshold (5 blocks in 10s) activates on ~100% of OPENs — degenerating to 'skip all OPENs', a known catastrophic failure mode. The mechanism is empirically refuted before implementation.

proposer.mechanism: ROLLING-WINDOW WIN-RATE COOLDOWN, layered on position-tier-gate (cap=1) verbatim. The exec algorithm overrides on_position_closed() to receive position-close events (Nautilus standard hook — verified available on ExecAlgorithm base class; same hook r2 attempted but with a different trigger). On each position close, it pushes a boolean (is_win = realized_pnl > 0) into a rolling deque of length WR_WINDOW (default 100). On each on_order() for an OPEN that survives the cap=1 gate, if the deque is full AND the rolling win-rate (mean of the deque) is below WR_THRESHOLD (default 0.32), SKIP the OPEN. Otherwise SUBMIT. CLOSE orders (is_reduce_only=True) always submit unchanged. Warmup: until the deque is full, the cooldown is inactive (SUBMIT). On session reset (per-date subprocess), the deque is cleared.
proposer.inefficiency_exploited: Win-rate REGIME variation across the train window. Empirically pre-validated via offline analysis of position-tier-gate positions.csv across all 12 train dates (90,433 positions, total realized_pnl $4,262.50): the rolling 100-position win-rate ranges from ~20% to ~55% within each session, and the subset of OPENs preceded by a 100-position window with win-rate < 0.32 has CONCRETELY NEGATIVE aggregate PnL (-$188.75 over 23,019 trades = -$0.0082/trade, vs the overall +$0.047/trade). Skipping that subset yields kept_pnl=$4,451.25 = +4.43% vs base. Per-date pattern: HELPS on 7 of 12 dates (20260311 +3.0, 20260312 +12.5, 20260313 +42.2, 20260315 +8.5, 20260316 +106.5, 20260317 +44.8, 20260319 +22.5); HURTS on 2 of 12 (20260318 -23.5, 20260320 -27.8); 3 dates have no skips (warmup-truncated). The signal is robust: 5 nearby parameterizations all produce delta in [+2.8%, +4.7%] range, with the chosen point being the most consistent (7/2 help/hurt ratio). Why this works mechanically: the oracle (sigma=6.0, R^2~14%) has time-varying realized accuracy; in 100-position windows where it has achieved <32% win rate, it is in a noisier regime and the next signals are disproportionately likely to also lose.
proposer.why_survives_costs: Mean slippage = 0 and commissions = 0 in this simulator (verified from base position-tier-gate backtest-results.json: mean_slippage=0.0, max_abs_slippage=0.0, total_commissions=0.0). The mechanism only adds a SKIP condition on OPEN orders that survive the cap=1 gate — no order construction, no order modification, no new order types, no passive orders, no market-data subscriptions. CLOSE orders submit unchanged so intraday_flat compliance is preserved. Runtime overhead: O(1) per OPEN (sum of deque divided by length, or maintained-running-sum equivalent) + O(1) per close (one deque push/pop). No dependency on simulator-delivered sub-second market data — the signal source is the algorithm's own running record of CLOSED position outcomes, which is delivered via Nautilus's reliable on_position_closed hook (r2 used the same hook with a different trigger; the hook itself fires reliably per the r2 outcome of -6.1% which proved the hook works, just that r2's trigger was the wrong axis).
proposer.builds_on: position-tier-gate (cap=1 retained verbatim as the first gate; rolling-WR cooldown is an additive SKIP gate applied AFTER cap=1 passes, only for OPEN orders). Structurally distinct from all 5 prior PC runs AND from round-1's chop-cooldown: r1 (consensus filter on order directions, inert at K=5/0.6); r2 (loss-cooldown after single position pnl<0, -6.1% because losses are i.i.d. at the single-trade level); r3 (winners-run extend-close, -82% because oracle reversal signals are real); r4 (adverse-mom via quote_tick, -3.1% because quote_tick under-fires); r5 (adverse-mom via book_deltas, 0.0% because delta channel was also under-fire); r6-round-1 (cap-block-density chop signal, empirically refuted because the signal is mechanically constant at 1/sec). This proposal differs from all of these by conditioning on the AGGREGATE win-rate over a wide rolling window — a noise-averaged regime signal that is NOT directly determined by either the oracle's fixed 1Hz cadence (which is uniform) or the per-trade pnl distribution (which is i.i.d. at the single-trade level). The win-rate at the 100-position window scale aggregates 100 i.i.d. trials and IS regime-sensitive (per the empirical 7/2 help/hurt pattern).
proposer.alternatives_considered: Empirically tested in offline pre-validation (all reported deltas measured on the 12-date train window via positions.csv analysis): (1) prior single position pnl<0 (r2 reproduction): -37.14% — confirms r2's failure. (2) prior dur<2s AND prior pnl<0 (chop-position cooldown): -8.19%, hurts 10 of 12 dates. (3) prior dur<2s only: -21.5%, removes too many winners. (4) prior pnl < -2.5 (large loss only): -1.57%, signal too sparse. (5) prior pnl < -1: -13.34%, removes profitable winners that follow $-1 losses. (6) loss_streak >= 3: -10.53%, loss streaks are uncorrelated with regime quality. (7) loss_streak >= 5: -1.33%, less harmful but still negative. (8) Late-session SKIP (criticizer suggestion): -0.2% to -0.7% across various N-minute thresholds; late-session positions have slightly positive pnl, not negative. (9) UTC-hour-based filter (skip 'negative-pnl' hours): +1.23% to +0.65% depending on hour set, all below gate. (10) Rolling N=50 wr<0.25: +1.96%. (11) Rolling N=100 wr<0.30: +3.51%. (12) Rolling N=200 wr<0.35: +4.67% (slightly higher headline than chosen but per-date pattern is 5/4 less robust than chosen N=100 wr<0.32's 7/2). (13) Rolling-window total-pnl-sum threshold: all variants gave -8% to +0.7%, weaker than win-rate. (14) Tighter threshold N=100 wr<0.30 (+3.51%) and wider N=100 wr<0.35 (+2.99%): both weaker. The chosen parameters (N=100, wr<0.32) are the sweet spot with the strongest help/hurt ratio (7/2). (15) Gap-based skip: positions all have gap>=1s by cap=1 construction; no sub-1s skip events exist. (16) Direction-based skip: positions.csv side field is always 'FLAT' (netting OMS), direction not directly inspectable.
proposer.revision_notes: Round 1 BLOCKING #1 (cap-block density signal is mechanically constant): ABANDONED entirely. The chop-block-density signal was empirically refuted by Criticizer's analysis showing ~100% activation rate. New mechanism uses a fundamentally different signal: rolling-window win-rate from position outcomes, which IS time-varying within sessions. Round 1 BLOCKING #2 (cap-blocks reflect oracle cadence, not chop): ABANDONED entirely with the same fix. Round 1 MAJOR (near-duplicate of r3): no longer applies — the new mechanism is parameterized to skip only ~25% of OPENs, NOT all OPENs. Round 1 MAJOR (lack of empirical pre-validation): FULLY ADDRESSED. This revision includes a complete sweep of 30+ candidate rules with their offline deltas and per-date breakdowns. The chosen rule's offline delta is +4.43% with 7/2 help/hurt — the most disciplined candidate selection in this experiment to date. Round 1 MAJOR (superior alternative — late-session forced exit): TESTED EMPIRICALLY and rejected — late-session OPENs have slightly positive pnl, so skipping them HURTS (deltas -0.2% to -0.7%). Round 1 MINOR (block-counter implementation surface): no longer applicable. Acknowledged limitation: the chosen rule's offline +4.43% is BELOW the +5% pass gate, but within the close_margin (close = within 2% of gate). Live result may be ±1-2% from offline due to per-date noise; realistic outcome distribution covers both PASS and CLOSE.

objections.text: Feedback-loop / selection-bias confound in the offline pre-validation. The +4.43% offline measurement was computed on the BASE-PTG position sequence — i.e., the rolling 100-position WR window at each decision point includes positions that the actual algorithm WOULD SKIP if the rule were active. In live execution, the deque only fills with positions that the algorithm DID NOT SKIP — a different, biased sub-sequence. Specifically, the algorithm skips positions where rolling-WR<0.32 (i.e., it removes a subset weighted toward losses), which RAISES the live rolling-WR above the offline-computed WR — meaning the activation rate in live will be LOWER than the 25.5% offline figure, and the skipped subset will be smaller. The realistic live delta could be anywhere from ~+0% (filter barely activates because skipping losers raises the visible WR above threshold) to the full +4.43% (if the WR signal is dominated by true regime structure not noise). Without iterating the offline simulation to convergence under the proposed rule, we don't know which. This is a well-known reflexivity pitfall in trading-rule backtesting that the Proposer should explicitly acknowledge.

Threshold-fit and parameter-search overfitting. The Proposer ran a sweep of 30+ (N, threshold) pairs and reported deltas in the [+0%, +4.7%] range. The chosen point (N=100, wr<0.32) is the 'sweet spot' with highest help/hurt ratio (7/2). But: (a) the OOS test window is a different 10 dates with potentially different regime structure, and (b) nearby parameter points have nontrivial spread: N=100 wr<0.30 gives +3.51%, wr<0.35 gives +2.99% — the optimum is locally peaked, not a flat plateau. A classic overfit signature. The realistic OOS-expected delta is probably 50-70% of the headline +4.43%, i.e. +2% to +3% — well below the +5% gate. The Proposer's own acknowledgment that the result is below the gate but 'within close_margin' is honest but understates the variance. The realistic outcome distribution centers below the gate.

Per-date pattern interpretation. The Proposer reports 7 help / 2 hurt for the chosen rule, but 3 of the 12 dates are noted as 'no skips (warmup-truncated)' — those dates are the LOW-VOLUME train dates (20260308 with 253 positions, 20260309 with 757, 20260310 with 436, all of which never fill a 100-position warmup window before late session). The rule is effectively inactive on those dates, contributing 0 to delta. The +4.43% is therefore concentrated in the high-volume late-window dates (20260316, 20260317, 20260319). The 12-date split is 3-no-effect / 7-help / 2-hurt, NOT a robust 7/2 majority. On OOS, if test dates resemble the low-volume early dates, the rule is inactive and delta is 0; if they resemble the high-volume late dates, delta could be larger but with the same per-day variance. The aggregate is regime-dependent.

on_position_closed hook semantics not fully verified for SKIPPED positions. The mechanism updates the deque only on on_position_closed events. But — does on_position_closed fire on the exec algo's own SKIPPED positions? Almost certainly NOT (a skipped OPEN never creates a position, so no PositionClosed event is emitted for it). This is structurally fine for the algorithm's intent (we only want to track ACTUAL trades the algo took), but it means the live position sequence is DIFFERENT from the offline base-PTG sequence (the latter has positions for every OPEN that survived cap=1). This compounds the round-2 MAJOR #1 feedback-loop concern. The offline pre-validation methodology should be replaced with a proper bootstrap: simulate the rule on the base-PTG order stream (not position stream), tracking which positions are skipped, and iterate. The Proposer has not done this — the +4.43% number is computed on a sequence the live algorithm will not actually see.

Superior alternative not considered: a strictly more conservative parameterization with a confirmed offline lower bound. Specifically, rolling N=200 wr<0.32 was empirically tested at +3.77% with help/hurt=5/3 — a slightly more disciplined signal (longer averaging window) at slightly lower headline delta. Or rolling N=250 wr<0.32 at +4.26% with help/hurt=4/4 — same headline-vs-base-rate trade-off. The N=100 choice maximizes the SAMPLED headline but the underlying signal is more sensitive to recent noise. A criticizer-recommended substitution would be N=200 wr<0.30 at +2.76% — explicitly lower headline but more bias-resistant. The Proposer should choose between (a) the headline-optimized N=100 wr<0.32 (this proposal, +4.43% offline, lower realistic OOS lift) or (b) a more bias-resistant N=200 wr<0.30 (+2.76% offline, lower headline but higher realistic OOS lift) — and provide an empirical rationale for the choice. Currently the Proposer just picked the highest help/hurt ratio without considering the bias trade-off.

The Proposer's failure-mode boundedness analysis is honest but should be made explicit in NOTES.md: if the feedback loop neutralizes the signal, the worst case is delta=0 (matching r5's outcome). The mechanism cannot regress slippage or commissions (both 0). It can only either help by skipping true loser-cluster trades, OR be inert if the WR signal doesn't transfer. The downside is structurally bounded — no -82% (r3) or -37% (r2 reproduction) catastrophe possible because the activation rate is bounded to ~25% offline and likely lower live.

Implementation specifics: the deque should store booleans (True/False for win) and a running sum (for O(1) WR computation), or use collections.deque + sum() per OPEN. Either is fine. The win-rate threshold check should be 'wr < threshold' (strict less-than) per the empirical analysis. The deque must be initialized empty in __init__ and cleared in on_reset for cross-date subprocess robustness. WR_WINDOW=100 and WR_THRESHOLD=0.32 should be configurable kwargs in the factory function so future iterations can tune without re-implementation. None of these are gating concerns, just polish.

suggested_alternatives: Use N=200 wr<0.30 (+2.76% offline) instead of N=100 wr<0.32 (+4.43%). The wider window gives a more bias-resistant estimator at lower headline delta. If the feedback-loop concern (round-2 MAJOR #1) dominates live, the wider-window version may actually produce a higher live delta because its rolling-WR is less affected by recent skip-induced WR upticks.

Run a proper feedback-loop offline simulation: iteratively apply the rule to the base-PTG order stream (NOT the position-completed sequence), removing skipped positions from the WR deque, and re-measure delta. This would give an unbiased estimate of the live delta and resolve round-2 MAJOR #1.

Pivot to a CLOSE-side mechanism that doesn't have the feedback-loop issue: e.g., when on_position_closed fires AND the just-closed position was a loss AND the rolling 100-window WR is below threshold, raise the cap to 2 for the NEXT order only (allow a same-direction add-on). This combines regime detection with sizing rather than skipping. But the base algo's empirical finding that the oracle never holds >1 contract means cap=2 would be inert in practice. Declined here, mentioned for completeness.
criticizer.reasoning: The mechanism is logically coherent, has documented empirical pre-validation (a discipline improvement over r1, r2, r3, r5-round-1), uses a reliable Nautilus hook (on_position_closed, verified working in r2), and has bounded downside (worst case = base PTG behavior, no slippage or commission regression possible). The remaining concerns are MAJOR but not BLOCKING: the feedback-loop bias is real and acknowledged, the parameter-search overfit risk is real and acknowledged, the per-date pattern is concentrated in high-volume dates rather than uniform. The realistic offline-to-live delta translation likely puts the live result in [+1%, +4%] — close to the gate but possibly below it (likely CLOSE rather than PASS). However, NO alternative mechanism has been identified that would clearly outperform this one on the position-tier-gate axis after 5 prior empirical failures. The Proposer should choose the parameterization with the best bias-resistance tradeoff (N=200 wr<0.30 is a worthy alternative to the headline N=100 wr<0.32) but either is acceptable. Ship the headline rule with explicit acknowledgment that offline-to-live divergence is the dominant risk and the realistic outcome is CLOSE rather than PASS in expectation.

final_hypothesis.why_survives_costs: Mean slippage = 0 and commissions = 0 in this simulator (verified from base position-tier-gate backtest-results.json). The mechanism only adds a SKIP condition on OPEN orders that survive the cap=1 gate — no order construction, no order modification, no new order types, no passive orders, no market-data subscriptions. CLOSE orders submit unchanged so intraday_flat compliance is preserved. Runtime overhead: O(1) per OPEN (running-sum maintained) + O(1) per close (one deque push/pop). No dependency on simulator-delivered sub-second market data — the signal source is the algorithm's own running record of CLOSED position outcomes, delivered via the on_position_closed hook which is verified working on ExecAlgorithm (r2 used the same hook and its -6.1% outcome confirmed the hook fires reliably).
final_hypothesis.builds_on: position-tier-gate (cap=1 retained verbatim as the first gate; rolling-WR cooldown is an additive SKIP gate applied AFTER cap=1 passes, only for OPEN orders). Structurally distinct from all 5 prior PC runs: r1 (consensus filter, inert); r2 (single-position loss-cooldown, -6.1% because losses are i.i.d. at the SINGLE-TRADE level); r3 (winners-run extend-close, -82%); r4 (adverse-mom via quote_tick, -3.1%); r5 (adverse-mom via book_deltas, 0.0%); and from round-1's chop-cooldown (empirically refuted as mechanically constant). This proposal differs by conditioning on the AGGREGATE win-rate over a 100-position rolling window — a noise-averaged regime signal that is NOT directly determined by either the oracle's fixed 1Hz cadence (uniform) or the per-trade pnl distribution (i.i.d. at single-trade level). The win-rate at the 100-position scale aggregates 100 i.i.d. trials and IS empirically regime-sensitive.
final_hypothesis.alternatives_considered: Empirically tested in offline pre-validation (deltas measured on the 12-date train window via positions.csv): (1) prior single position pnl<0 (r2 reproduction): -37.14%. (2) prior dur<2s AND prior pnl<0: -8.19%. (3) prior dur<2s only: -21.5%. (4) prior pnl < -2.5: -1.57%. (5) loss_streak>=3: -10.53%, >=5: -1.33%, >=7: -0.32%. (6) Late-session SKIP (criticizer suggestion): -0.2% to -0.7% across various N-minute thresholds. (7) UTC-hour filter (skip negative-pnl hours): +0.65% to +1.23%, all below gate. (8) Rolling-window total-pnl-sum threshold: all variants -8% to +0.7%. (9) Adjacent rolling-WR parameterizations: N=200 wr<0.30 (+2.76%, more bias-resistant); N=200 wr<0.35 (+4.67% headline but 5/4 help/hurt, less consistent than chosen N=100 wr<0.32 at 7/2). The chosen point optimizes empirical help/hurt consistency.
